claims.claim: The American Marketing Association's working definition: marketing is the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large.

When people are asked what marketing is, most answer advertising or selling; both are part of marketing, but marketing is much more — it includes every process involved in moving an offering from the organization to the consumer, starting with discerning customer needs.

Marketing and sales are different jobs: sales incorporates actually selling the company's products or services to customers, while marketing is the process of communicating the value of a product or service to customers so that the product or service sells.

The value idea: marketing is finding out the needs and wants of potential buyers — organizations or consumers — and then providing goods and services that meet or exceed the expectations of those buyers.

The exchange idea: marketing is about creating exchanges, and an exchange takes place when two parties give something of value to each other to satisfy their respective needs or wants; typical exchanges trade money for a good or service, but some are nonmonetary.

The marketing mix is the set of tools marketers combine, classically the four Ps — product (what is offered: a good, a service, or an idea), price (what the customer gives in exchange), place (how the offering reaches the customer), and promotion (how the organization informs and influences, including advertising, public relations, and social media); the mix is only as good as its weakest element.

Marketing is not a business-only activity: the AMA definition assigns value to customers, clients, partners, and society at large, and every organization with people to serve and something to offer — universities, food banks, hospitals, agencies — creates, communicates, delivers, and exchanges value.

The marketing concept is the use of marketing data to focus on the needs and wants of customers in order to develop strategies that satisfy customer needs and accomplish the goals of the organization; marketing that lasts is marketing where the customer genuinely wins.

CFI describes marketing as the business activities associated with communicating, advertising, delivering, or selling products or services to customers, with the goal of drawing consumers' attention and creating a relationship with existing customers — corroborating that marketing spans far more than advertising.
Customer satisfaction is the customer's feeling that a product has met or exceeded expectations, which is why exchanges repeat when the offer genuinely meets a need.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many Ps are in the marketing mix?
positions: The classic framework names four Ps: product, price, place, promotion.
Some textbooks extend the mix — OpenStax's Introduction to Business adds 'People' to make five Ps, and services marketing adds Physical Evidence and Process.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the classic four Ps as the standard naming, mentions the mix only to make the definition intelligible, and leaves the full framework to the marketing-mix sibling topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which definition of marketing is canonical?
positions: The AMA defines marketing as the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large.

OpenStax's Introduction to Business defines marketing by the 'right' principle (getting the right goods, services, or ideas to the right people at the right place, time, and price, using the right promotion techniques), and CFI defines it as business activities of communicating, advertising, delivering, or selling.
OpenStax's Principles of Marketing quotes the AMA definition verbatim.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson anchors on the AMA definition, quoted with attribution, because it is the professional body's official working definition and is corroborated by OpenStax's Principles of Marketing; the other formulations are compatible and used only as corroboration.

positions: A cynical view: marketing is getting people to buy things they do not need.
The marketing concept: marketing uses customer-need information to build strategies that satisfy customers and accomplish the organization's goals at the same time.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the marketing concept and the honest framing — marketing works when the customer wins too — without policy positions or manipulation content.
